title: Examining (Political) Content Consumption on Facebook Through Data Donation
screen_reason: The paper's aim is political-content consumption on Facebook via data donation (1,261 US users, 32M posts from their donated public pages/groups, Oct 2022-Sep 2023), but it reports one quantitative misinformation share with a denominator: low-quality / 'fake news' URLs (Media Bias Fact Check domain list) constituted 'less than 0.01% of the total urls shared'. Per the rule that a study with another aim is still included if a descriptive share is reported anywhere, this is eligible - though only as a bound, not a point estimate.

estimates.platform: Facebook (public pages and groups, via donated account data enriched with CrowdTangle)
estimates.measure_type: % of URLs in the donated Facebook page/group post corpus that were low-quality or 'fake news' domains
estimates.value_raw: less than 0.01% of the total urls shared
estimates.denominator: All URLs in the 32,026,862 posts (16,633,666 English) collected from a random 10% sample of the 251,220 public pages/groups donated by 1,261 American Facebook users; the URL count itself is not stated
estimates.definition: A URL whose domain appears on the Media Bias Fact Check list of low-quality / 'fake news' sources (as compiled by Weld, Glenski and Althoff 2021)
estimates.misinfo_def: The paper gives no formal definition; it speaks of 'low-quality or fake news URLs' and of 'domains known for low-quality content'
estimates.n: Total URLs shared in the post corpus (count not reported); corpus = 32,026,862 posts from 1,261 users' pages/groups
estimates.source_quote: Additionally, we investigated the prevalence of low-quality or 'fake news' URLs using sources listed by Media Bias Fact Check (Weld, Glenski, and Althoff 2021), finding them to constitute less than 0.01% of the total urls shared.
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Third-party domain list: Media Bias Fact Check ratings as compiled by Weld, Glenski & Althoff (2021); the authors also used Robertson et al. (2018) domain-level leaning scores for the bias analysis. No coder reliability and no count of matched URLs reported
estimates.moderator_quote: The final dataset, comprises 32,026,862 posts published between October 2022 and September 2023. Of those, 16,633,666 are tagged as English according to CrowdTangle's 'language code' field.
estimates.notes: Only an upper bound ('less than 0.01%'), so value_kind = range_not_point and value_pct is empty. Coded EXPOSURE/diet_share because the corpus is anchored to individual donors' own pages/groups and the whole paper frames it as their consumption diet, weighted to population level. A reasonable coder could instead call this CONTENT: the posts were pulled from CrowdTangle for every donated page/group whether or not the donor ever saw them, and the authors concede the data 'may not accurately represent the full spectrum of information that users are exposed to'. denom_scope = all_media because the denominator is every URL in the corpus (lifestyle, entertainment, religion, sport as well as news), not a news- or topic-restricted set. topic coded general_news as the closest fit for an unrestricted diet; English-language posts only.

missed_or_uncertain: (1) The paper's headline number - 'around 17% of the content being consumed is political content', with demographic splits (Hispanics ~14%, Asians/Whites ~20%, 18-24 12%, 65+ 24%) - is political-content prevalence, not misinformation, so no row. (2) URL ideological bias (Figure 6, a centrist distribution with a slight rightward skew) is slant, not veracity: not extractable under the construct rules. (3) Topic/format shares (lifestyle, entertainment, religion; photo/video/text fractions by age and ethnicity) are unrelated to misinformation. (4) No count of matched low-quality URLs, and no denominator count of URLs, is given anywhere, so the 0.01% bound cannot be turned into a part/whole share. (5) The misinformation sentence is a single aside; the authors themselves say 'the topic of misinformation, while touched upon briefly in this paper, warrants a deeper investigation'. A coder who required a point estimate rather than a bound could defensibly screen this paper EXCLUDE.

rob.design: Opt-in data donation. 1,261 US Facebook users recruited through the PureSpectrum survey panel donated their public pages/groups (251,220 entities: ~210,000 pages, ~42,000 groups) and answered a 5-question demographic survey; a random 10% of entities was queried via CrowdTangle, yielding 32,026,862 posts (16,633,666 English) published Oct 2022-Sep 2023. Convenience sample (women over-represented, 18-24 under-represented) reweighted to population level with inverse propensity scores using Facebook's 'balance' library. Political content detected by a fine-tuned BERT classifier (AUC-ROC 0.951 on held-out data; distant labels validated on 250 random posts per class: 97% of political-page posts political, 98% of non-political-page posts non-political). Misinformation measured only by matching URL domains to a Media Bias Fact Check list; no response rate, no inter-coder reliability, no numerator/denominator counts. Stated limitations: English only; public pages/groups only, which 'does not necessarily encompass the entirety of content users encounter on their feeds'.
rob.item6_quote: Additionally, we investigated the prevalence of low-quality or 'fake news' URLs using sources listed by Media Bias Fact Check (Weld, Glenski, and Althoff 2021), finding them to constitute less than 0.01% of the total urls shared.
rob.item10_quote: Additionally, we investigated the prevalence of low-quality or 'fake news' URLs using sources listed by Media Bias Fact Check (Weld, Glenski, and Althoff 2021), finding them to constitute less than 0.01% of the total urls shared. This minimal presence suggests effective moderation by Facebook of domains known for low-quality content, aligning with the platform's policies against misinformation.
